note: Per-build expected enablement behavior for Microsoft's native NVMe driver on Windows client. First matching rule wins (rules are ordered most-specific first). 'expectedPath' values: registry-override | vivetool-fallback | none-known | official-optin. Microsoft changes this behavior out-of-band — update this file (an administrator-owned copy in %ProgramData%\NVMePatcher\State takes precedence over the bundled one).

rules.summary: Windows Server 2025: native NVMe is an official, supported opt-in feature (GA after the October 2025 cumulative). Use Microsoft's documented enablement, not client-style overrides.

Build 26300+ (26H2 Experimental) ships a native 'Feature flags' page (Settings > Windows Update > Windows Insider Program), confirmed in Microsoft's own release notes. Check there first: Microsoft may expose native NVMe as an official toggle, which is preferable to these overrides. As of the 2026-10-05 review it isn't listed there, and the GenNvmeDisk compatible ID is still removed on these trains (ViVe issue 164), so the registry and ViVeTool routes don't bind the driver. Treat this tool as verify/monitor/rollback until an official toggle appears.

Insider trains newer than 26200 (26H1 28020/28120 and later) inherit the GenNvmeDisk compatible-ID removal, so no working enablement path is known. Candidate probe 48613417 (NativeNVMeStackEnableForClientOS) is untested on this branch; source: https://github.com/phantomofearth/windows-velocity-feature-lists. Applying it remains gated behind live validation. Wait for Microsoft's official client rollout. 26H1 is an OEM-only, ARM-targeted release and does not get Hotpatch.

Evidenced on Insider 26200.8524 (ViVe issue 164): stornvme stopped exposing the GenNvmeDisk compatible ID, so nvmedisk.inf can't match and both the registry and ViVeTool routes set flags that have no effect. Retail 25H2 UBRs above 8524 have no exact sourced evidence either way, so they stay verify/monitor/rollback. Candidate probe 48613417 (NativeNVMeStackEnableForClientOS) is untested on this branch; source: https://github.com/phantomofearth/windows-velocity-feature-lists. Applying it remains gated behind live validation. No working enablement path is known; wait for Microsoft's official client rollout. A host that reports 26H2 is an enablement package over 25H2, so it keeps build 26200 and lands on this rule.

25H2 (26200.x before .8524): the registry override is neutered, and the FeatureStore fallback applies 55369237 + 48433719 (49453572 is Always Enabled and probe-only). One forum report also has 60786016 + 48433719 binding on 26200.8116/.8117; this set doesn't use it. A host that reports 26H2 is an enablement package over 25H2, so it keeps build 26200 and lands on the 25H2 rules.

Windows 11 build 26100.8106 is where the original FeatureManagement override set stopped binding, while the FeatureStore fallback was reported working. A newer three-value override set has since been reported binding on 26100.8457 and 26100.9550 (see the 24H2 rule below). This exact rule must not be extrapolated to adjacent UBRs.

No Microsoft client matrix covers 24H2, and no exact rule is sourced for this build/UBR. Forum reports have overrides 3244671118 + 1853569164 + 156965516 binding nvmedisk on 26100.8457 and 26100.9550. A test install of 26100.9550 confirmed the bind and showed the costs: Windows deletes the 735209102 override at boot, binding needed all three values, and 156965516 makes DISM /ScanHealth report component store corruption while it's set (SFC stays clean, and the report clears once the value is removed). Verify, monitor, or roll back only; don't extrapolate from 26100.8106.

Pre-24H2 client builds have no sourced working enablement interval and may lack complete native NVMe components. The tool is verify/monitor/rollback-only; writing override keys is not evidence that the driver can bind.
